title: Not a single word written by Socrates survives: we know him only through others

cover.alt: A marble bust of Socrates with a broad, snub-nosed face, a bald crown and a thick curly beard, in the Vatican’s Pio-Clementino Museum.

body: No writings by Socrates have come down to us, so his views have to be pieced together from other people’s accounts. The main ones come from Plato and Xenophon, from the comic playwright Aristophanes, and from Aristotle, and they do not always agree. Plato’s Socrates says he never took money for teaching; Xenophon’s says his students pay him. Plato also seems to have used Socrates as a voice for his own ideas, and very few, if any, of his dialogues are word-for-word records. Telling the historical man apart from the literary character is known as the Socratic problem.

slides.heading: The four main witnesses
items: Xenophon: his own Apology and Symposium
Aristotle: notes on what Socrates taught

left.label: Plato’s Socrates
left.text: Denies ever having accepted money to teach anyone.

right.label: Xenophon’s Socrates
right.text: In Xenophon’s Symposium, he says his students pay him for teaching wisdom.

slides.question: Which of these early accounts of Socrates was a comedy written to make fun of him?
slides.explanation: Aristophanes’ Clouds, staged in 423 BC, humorously attacks Socrates. The others are Socratic works by Plato or Xenophon.

slides.heading: Whose ideas are they?
slides.text: Many of Plato’s dialogues seem to use Socrates as a device for Plato’s own thought. Aristotle offers a clue: he says Socrates did not hold that the Forms exist separately, the famous theory most associated with Plato, and that Socrates focused on defining concepts.

slides.alt: Jacques-Louis David’s painting The Death of Socrates: Socrates sits upright on a bed, one hand raised, reaching for a cup while grieving followers surround him.
slides.caption: Jacques-Louis David’s The Death of Socrates imagines his last hours. He was put to death by the democracy of Athens in 399 BC.

slides.clue: The comic playwright who mocked Socrates on stage in 423 BC
slides.detail: Aristophanes is one of the four main sources on Socrates, alongside Plato, Xenophon and Aristotle.
